summary: Presents a framework for inter-domain route aggregation, showing how routes can be combined to keep global routing tables smaller, with an example router configuration. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Instead of writing every street on a map, you can write just the town. This document explains how routers do something like that to keep their lists short.

subtitle: A scalable strategy for keeping routing tables small as the Internet grows

tldr.problem: The Internet routing table grows exponentially as more organizations connect and announce their networks, consuming memory and CPU time on routers worldwide and slowing route calculations.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC proposes a framework where each organization aggregates its own routes before announcing them to the Internet, and uses BGP's 'no-export' community to prevent certain detailed routes from propagating unnecessarily, allowing upstream providers to announce smaller aggregates.
tldr.outcome: Route aggregation by the source, applied consistently at all levels of the routing hierarchy, can significantly reduce routing table size and growth rate while still allowing organizations flexibility in their internal routing.

facts.label: Scope
facts.value: Applied recursively at all network hierarchy levels

today: RFC 2519 is an Informational RFC and has not been obsoleted. The framework it describes remains the basis for BGP route aggregation practice on the modern Internet, helping manage the growth of the global routing table.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Route aggregation is the practice of combining multiple IP network routes into fewer, larger routes. When an organization controls multiple network prefixes, it can announce a single, larger prefix instead of dozens of smaller ones. This reduces the size of the Internet routing table, which directly saves memory and CPU resources on routers worldwide.

The RFC cites two major achievements in route aggregation: standardized address allocation policies from regional registries that follow CIDR (Classless Inter-Domain Routing) principles, which made aggregation technically possible, and route aggregation by large 'Tier 1' providers, which achieved the biggest reductions in routing table size.

However, not all organizations implement aggregation effectively, so the routing table continues to grow unsustainably. This RFC establishes a clearly defined framework based on current Internet practice, emphasizing aggregation by the source: each organization should aggregate its own routes before announcing them to other networks, using the BGP 'no-export' community to give organizations control over what their upstream providers propagate.
sections.eli5: Routers keep lists of all the networks on the Internet. If the list gets too big, routers slow down. Organizations can make the list shorter by announcing one big route instead of many small ones.

sections.title: The Route Aggregation Framework
sections.content:
The framework has two main principles. First, aggregation from the originating AS: each Autonomous System (AS, essentially one organization's routing domain) aggregates the BGP routes it originates and announces a smaller number of larger prefixes. This gives the originating AS control over the granularity of routing information it sends out.

Second, using BGP community 'no-export' toward upstream providers: when an AS announces routes to its provider, it can tag certain routes with the 'no-export' community attribute, signaling that those routes should not be propagated beyond the provider's network. This is useful for routes that are only relevant locally or to the provider.

The framework applies recursively at all levels: Tier 1 providers aggregate their routes for both peer providers and customers; Tier 2 providers aggregate their own routes, tag some with 'no-export', and announce customer routes; and so on down the hierarchy. This distributed approach avoids the complexity of coordinating aggregation across many organizations.
sections.eli5: Each organization announces one big route instead of many small ones. And it can tell its provider 'do not tell anyone else about this route'.

sections.title: How Organizations Aggregate
sections.content:
Within its own network, an organization should advertise the large address blocks allocated by its provider or from a registry, then allocate subnets to specific access routers. For example, a /17 prefix can be divided into /20 prefixes for different access routers, which can then allocate /22 or /24 prefixes to customer connections. Inside the AS, only the /20 routes need to be announced; the smaller /22 and /24 routes stay local unless they are multi-homed (connected through multiple paths).

To other AS's, the organization should announce its large blocks and suppress the more-specific routes. However, routes originating from customer AS's should be advertised to upstream providers. The organization uses 'no-export' on routes that do not need wider propagation, such as a customer's subnet that is singly-homed or used only for backup, or a more-specific route used locally for load balancing.

The 'no-export' attribute is powerful because it gives control to the AS originating the route, avoiding the need for complex coordination among multiple organizations for proxy aggregation.
sections.eli5: Inside the organization, announce the big blocks, not the small ones. To the outside world, announce the big blocks and mark the small ones 'do not propagate beyond my provider'.

sections.title: Provider Responsibilities
sections.content:
Providers must aggregate consistently toward all their peers and customers to avoid routing instabilities. Announcing different levels of detail to different peers (such as announcing full routes to some customers but aggregates to others) can cause serious routing problems because of longest-match routing: a router following the longest matching prefix may choose different next-hops for traffic to different subnets within the same block, breaking traffic flow.

Every effort must be made to ensure consistent route aggregation. This means deploying filtering on BGP peers that receive full, non-aggregated routes, so that even customers who want detailed routing information receive only the aggregates.

A provider aggregates routes it originates and respects the 'no-export' community on customer routes. It does not aggregate routes from other providers or from customers it peers with (those routes are advertised as received), so it cannot reduce routing table size for traffic to those networks, but it maintains consistency and stability.
sections.eli5: Providers tell everyone the same aggregated routes. If someone needs more detail, they get filtered routes at the edge, not different versions everywhere.

sections.title: Example: A Multi-Homed Customer
sections.content:
Consider a scenario with two Tier 1 providers. AS 1000 (a Tier 1) owns large blocks 208.128.0.0/12 and 166.55.0.0/16. AS 2000 is a customer with a 'portable' address 160.75.0.0/16 (which it can move to another provider) and an address 208.128.0.0/19 allocated from AS 1000.

AS 1000 announces its large blocks and suppresses more-specific routes. It advertises the routes it receives from customer AS 2000. AS 2000 announces both 160.75.0.0/16 and 208.128.0.0/19 to its provider, tags the /19 with 'no-export', and suppresses more-specific routes. The /19 stays within AS 1000 (the 'no-export' community prevents propagation), while the /16 propagates through AS 1000 to the rest of the Internet.

This allows AS 2000 to be multi-homed (connected to AS 1000 via the /16, perhaps to another provider via different routes) while still participating in route aggregation. Without 'no-export', AS 1000 would either have to aggregate away the /19 (losing control) or announce both prefixes, growing the routing table.
sections.eli5: A customer can say 'announce this route only to my provider, keep it there'. This lets one customer connect to multiple providers without breaking route aggregation.

viz.caption: Aggregation hierarchy: each level combines routes before announcing

layers.label: Tier 1 providers
layers.detail: Announce aggregated routes to peers and customers

layers.label: Tier 2 providers
layers.detail: Aggregate their own routes, use no-export to providers

layers.label: Customer networks
layers.detail: Announce customer routes to provider, tag some as no-export

layers.label: Direct connections
layers.detail: Smaller networks announce detailed routes via no-export
